proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(L=L_m\) and \(a=a_m\).  We first record, and prove, the finite nested-neighborhood transport fact used below.  For row masses \((\rho_b)_{b=0}^H\) and column masses \((\sigma_w)_{w=0}^H\) of equal total mass, a nonnegative array supported on \(b+w\le H\) can have those margins only if
\[
 \sum_{b=h}^H\rho_b\le \sum_{w=0}^{H-h}\sigma_w,
 \qquad h=0,\ldots,H.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Conversely, (1) is sufficient.  Indeed, process rows \(b=H,H-1,\ldots,0\) and fill row \(b\) from the still available mass in columns \(0,\ldots,H-b\).  Before row \(b\) is filled, the already processed rows have consumed exactly \(\sum_{r>b}\rho_r\) units from that prefix.  Thus its residual mass is
\[
 \sum_{w=0}^{H-b}\sigma_w-\sum_{r>b}\rho_r\ge \rho_b
\]
by (1).  The row can therefore be filled.  At termination every row has its prescribed mass; equality of the total masses then forces every column to have its prescribed mass.  This proves sufficiency without a positivity or strict-slack condition.  Applied to \((p,q)\), the assumed nonemptiness of \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) therefore implies
\[
 A_s=\sum_{b=H-s}^Hp_b\le Q_s,\qquad s=0,\ldots,H.          \tag{2}
\]

Fix \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\) and set \(z_w=\sum_{b\ge m}x_{bw}\) and \(Z_s=\sum_{w=0}^sz_w\).  A selected row has \(b\ge m\), so its eligible columns satisfy \(w\le H-b\le H-m=L\).  Hence \(z_w=0\) for \(w>L\).  Nonnegativity and the column margins give \(0\le z_w\le q_w\), while the selected row margins give \(Z_L=a\).  Finally, rows \(b\ge H-s\) can use only columns \(w\le s\), and those rows are selected when \(s\le L\); consequently
\[
 Z_s\ge \sum_{b=H-s}^Hp_b=A_s,\qquad 0\le s\le L.          \tag{3}
\]

These conditions are also sufficient.  Suppose \(z\) obeys the displayed conditions in the theorem.  For the selected rows \(b=m,\ldots,H\), condition (1) at row cutoff \(h\ge m\) becomes
\[
 \sum_{b=h}^Hp_b=A_{H-h}\le Z_{H-h},                       \tag{4}
\]
which is exactly one of (3).  The constructive argument proving (1) therefore gives a selected-row transport with column margins \(z\).  For the complementary rows \(b<m\), the residual column margin is \(q-z\).  For \(h<m\), since \(H-h\ge L+1\) and \(z_w=0\) for \(w>L\), its Hall inequality is
\[
 \sum_{b=h}^{m-1}p_b
 =\sum_{b=h}^Hp_b-a
 \le Q_{H-h}-a
 =\sum_{w=0}^{H-h}(q_w-z_w),                               \tag{5}
\]
where the inequality is (2).  Thus the same constructive argument gives a complementary-row transport.  Adding the two transports gives an element of \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) inducing \(z\).  This proves the exact characterization of attainable selected subdistributions.

Every feasible cumulative array satisfies
\[
 Z_s\le a,\qquad Z_s\le Q_s,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 Z_s\le \min\{a,Q_s\}=Z_{ms}^{-}.                        \tag{6}
\]
The array \(Z_{ms}^{-}\) is itself feasible: its increments are nonnegative and bounded by the corresponding increments of \(Q\), its terminal value is \(a\), and (2), together with \(A_s\le a\), gives \(A_s\le Z_{ms}^{-}\).  It is therefore the pointwise maximal attainable cumulative array.

For the opposite extremum, if \(u\ge s\), then \(Z_u-Z_s\le Q_u-Q_s\) and \(Z_u\ge A_u\).  Hence every feasible array obeys
\[
 Z_s\ge Q_s+A_u-Q_u.
\]
Maximizing this inequality over \(u=s,\ldots,L\) gives \(Z_s\ge Z_{ms}^{+}\).  It remains to verify attainability of this simultaneous lower envelope.  Because \(A_L=a\),
\[
 Z_{mL}^{+}=Q_L+(A_L-Q_L)=a.                               \tag{7}
\]
Separating the term \(u=s\) from the defining maximum yields the backward recursion
\[
 Z_{ms}^{+}=\max\{A_s,Z_{m,s+1}^{+}-q_{s+1}\},
 \qquad s<L.                                               \tag{8}
\]
Since \(A_s\le A_{s+1}\le Z_{m,s+1}^{+}\), (8) implies \(Z_{ms}^{+}\le Z_{m,s+1}^{+}\); it also implies \(Z_{m,s+1}^{+}-Z_{ms}^{+}\le q_{s+1}\).  Moreover, (2) gives \(A_u-Q_u\le0\), so \(0\le Z_{m0}^{+}\le q_0\).  Thus the increments of \(Z_m^{+}\) lie between zero and the corresponding \(q_w\), (7) gives the required total mass, and (8) gives \(Z_{ms}^{+}\ge A_s\).  The exact characterization already proved makes \(Z_m^{+}\) attainable.  It is the pointwise minimal attainable cumulative array.

For any selected subdistribution supported on \(0,\ldots,L\), summation by parts gives
\[
 \sum_{w=0}^{L}wz_w
 =\sum_{s=0}^{L-1}\sum_{w=s+1}^{L}z_w
 =La-\sum_{s=0}^{L-1}Z_s.                                 \tag{9}
\]
The maximal cumulative array \(Z_m^{-}\) therefore minimizes (9), and the minimal cumulative array \(Z_m^{+}\) maximizes it.  Both values are attained by the transports constructed above.  Finally, the definition of \(J_m\), the fixed \((B,T)\) margin, and \(\mu_b=\sum_ttp_{bt}\) give
\[
 J_m=\pi\left\{\sum_{b<m}\mu_b+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right\}. \tag{10}
\]
Every attaining \(x\) extends to a triple coupling by \(\text{lem:triple-projection-and-extension}\), and \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) realizes that triple while preserving the observed law.  Thus (10) turns the two attained transport extrema into sharp causal, rather than merely algebraic, endpoints.  No division by \(a\) is used, so the argument includes \(a=0\); all formulas also remain valid at Hall equalities.

Let \(\gamma\in\mathcal G_H(p_{BT},q)\) and define \(x_{bw}=\sum_t\gamma_{btw}\).  Nonnegativity is immediate, and the first triple-margin constraint gives
\[
 \sum_wx_{bw}=\sum_{t,w}\gamma_{btw}=\sum_tp_{bt}=p_b.
\]
The second triple-margin constraint gives
\[
 \sum_bx_{bw}=\sum_{b,t}\gamma_{btw}=q_w.
\]
If \(b+w>H\), every summand \(\gamma_{btw}\) is zero, so \(x_{bw}=0\).  Hence the projection belongs to \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\).

Conversely, fix \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\).  If \(p_b=0\), nonnegativity and \(p_b=\sum_tp_{bt}\) imply \(p_{bt}=0\) for every \(t\), while the row constraint for \(x\) implies \(x_{bw}=0\) for every \(w\).  Set \(\gamma_{btw}=0\) on such rows.  If \(p_b>0\), set
\[
 \gamma_{btw}=\frac{p_{bt}x_{bw}}{p_b}.                    \tag{1}
\]
The denominator is strictly positive in precisely the case where (1) is used.  Then
\[
 \sum_w\gamma_{btw}
 =\frac{p_{bt}}{p_b}\sum_wx_{bw}=p_{bt},                  \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{b,t}\gamma_{btw}
 =\sum_{b:p_b>0}\frac{x_{bw}}{p_b}\sum_tp_{bt}
 =\sum_bx_{bw}=q_w.                                       \tag{3}
\]
Finally, \(x_{bw}=0\) when \(b+w>H\), so (1) has the required support.  Equations (1)--(3) prove that \(\gamma\in\mathcal G_H(p_{BT},q)\) and that its \((B,W)\) projection is exactly \(x\).  The displayed choice happens to make \(T\) and \(W\) conditionally independent given \(B\), but only existence of this extension is used; no such independence is imposed on general members of the triple polytope.

Let \(P_O\) be the stipulated observed distribution and let \(\mathsf P_0\in\mathfrak M_H\) be the particular admitted sustained-arm full-data extension named in the theorem.  Write \(U_0\) for its response table.  Because the horizon is finite and every raw-count coordinate is integer valued, the response-type space is countable; all conditional kernels used below therefore exist by elementary discrete disintegration.

First retain, jointly and without modification, the two sustained raw histories from \(U_0\).  On \(\{S_k^1=1,B=b,T=t\}\), define a conditional draw \(\widetilde W\) by
\[
 \mathsf P(\widetilde W=w\mid U_0)
 =\frac{\gamma_{btw}}{p_{bt}}\quad\text{when }p_{bt}>0.    \tag{1}
\]
When \(p_{bt}=0\), that conditioning event has probability zero and the conditional law may be chosen arbitrarily.  Since \(\sum_w\gamma_{btw}=p_{bt}\), (1) is a probability mass function.  Moreover,
\[
 \mathsf P(B=b,T=t,\widetilde W=w\mid S_k^1=1)
 =p_{bt}\frac{\gamma_{btw}}{p_{bt}}=\gamma_{btw}           \tag{2}
\]
on positive cells, and both sides vanish on zero cells.  Thus the desired triple margin is obtained.  Summing (2) over \(b,t\) gives
\[
 \mathsf P(\widetilde W=w\mid S_k^1=1)=q_w.               \tag{3}
\]

We next construct a legal switched raw history.  Through time \(k\), copy the sustained intensive history exactly.  If it is dead at \(k\), continue the absorbing death state and make no later count increment.  If it is alive at \(k\), keep it alive through \(K\), let its raw count jump by exactly \(\widetilde W\) at time \(k+1\), and keep the count constant thereafter.  This is well defined because \(K\ge k+1\), multiple events in one interval are allowed, and \(\widetilde W\in\mathbb I_H\).  It is nondecreasing, death is absorbing, and its raw post-landmark increment equals \(\widetilde W\).  Therefore its separately capped increment is also \(W=\widetilde W\).  The support restriction on \(\gamma\) gives
\[
 \mathsf P(B+W\le H\mid S_k^1=1)=1.                       \tag{4}
\]
Notice that if the retained raw count at \(k\) already exceeds \(H\), then \(B=H\), so (4) forces \(W=0\); the raw count itself is left unchanged and need not be bounded by \(H\).

To complete the whole finite response tree, index a node by its treatment prefix.  Put the retained sustained histories and the newly constructed switched history on their corresponding nodes.  These prescriptions agree whenever their treatment prefixes agree: in particular, the intensive and switched branches agree through \(k\) by construction, and the two retained sustained branches already came from the valid table \(U_0\).  Traverse all remaining prefix nodes in increasing time order.  At an unset child, copy its parent's count and death state; if the parent is alive, append a zero-event alive continuation, and if it is dead, append the absorbing state.  Because every node has a unique treatment prefix, this recursion assigns one state to each prefix and therefore enforces the FFRCISTG no-anticipation requirement.  It also preserves nondecreasing integer counts and absorbing death on every branch.  Denote the resulting table by \(U'\).  This is the explicit action of \(\mathfrak L\).

It remains to verify randomization, censoring, and the observed pushforward.  One convenient joint construction is to sample \((U_0,R,C)\) with its original law \(\mathsf P_0\), then sample the auxiliary draw in (1) conditionally on \(U_0\) but not on \(R\), and finally form \(U'\).  For every response-table event \(E\) and arm \(a\), baseline randomization under \(\mathsf P_0\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathsf P(U'\in E,R=a)
 &=\int \mathsf P(U'\in E\mid U_0=u)\,
       \mathsf P_0(R=a,U_0\in du)\\
 &=\mathsf P_0(R=a)\int \mathsf P(U'\in E\mid U_0=u)\,
       \mathsf P_0(U_0\in du)\\
 &=\mathsf P_0(R=a)\mathsf P(U'\in E).
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{5}
\]
Thus \(R\perp U'\), and the original positive assignment probabilities are retained.

For \(R=0\) or \(R=1\), the factual sustained branch of \(U'\) is exactly that of \(U_0\).  We also retain the original \(C\).  Consequently
\[
 (R,C,\mathcal H_K^R)\ \text{has exactly the same law under the construction as under }\mathsf P_0. \tag{6}
\]
Consistency then makes the path truncated at \(C\), and hence \(O\), identical under the two laws.  This proves preservation of the complete observed pushforward, not merely of a terminal summary.  Equation (6) also shows, for every factual at-risk history on which it is defined, that
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\mathsf P(C\ge\ell\mid R=a,C\ge\ell-1,D_{\ell-1}^a=0,
                    \mathcal H_K^a)\\
 &\qquad=\mathsf P_0(C\ge\ell\mid R=a,C\ge\ell-1,D_{\ell-1}^a=0,
                    \mathcal H_K^a)\\
 &\qquad=\mathsf P_0(C\ge\ell\mid R=a,C\ge\ell-1,D_{\ell-1}^a=0,
                    \mathcal H_{\ell-1}^a)\\
 &\qquad=\mathsf P(C\ge\ell\mid R=a,C\ge\ell-1,D_{\ell-1}^a=0,
                    \mathcal H_{\ell-1}^a),
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{7}
\]
where the middle equality is censoring exchangeability for \(\mathsf P_0\).  Positivity is retained because the common quantity in (7) is the original strictly positive continuation probability.  Equivalently, (6) may be generated by the original sequence of factual-history continuation kernels, including the original post-death convention.  Retaining the joint law in (6), rather than postulating an independence factorization for \(C\), makes clear that no independence of censoring from unassigned counterfactual branches is required.

Equations (2)--(7), together with the prefix construction, verify respectively the triple margin, capped residual transportability, capacity, no anticipation, absorbing death, baseline randomization, consistency, assignment and censoring positivity, sequential coarsening at random, and observed-law preservation.  These are exactly the restrictions defining \(\mathfrak M_H\).  The convenient auxiliary kernel in (1) may happen to create additional conditional independences in this particular witness, but none is assumed or required: one may couple unused-branch completion randomizers with \(\widetilde W\) while retaining (2)--(7), so the maintained class gains no cross-world independence restriction.

Conversely, let \(\mathsf P\in\mathfrak M_H\).  Define
\[
 \gamma_{btw}=\mathsf P(B=b,T=t,W=w\mid S_k^1=1).          \tag{8}
\]
Landmark-survival positivity makes this conditioning well defined.  Its \((B,T)\) margin is \(p_{bt}\); capped residual transportability makes its \(W\) margin \(q_w\); and capped capacity makes (8) vanish when \(b+w>H\).  Hence \(\gamma\in\mathcal G_H(p_{BT},q)\), proving the converse.

Fix the observed law \(P_O\).  Distinguish the causal identified set
\[
 \Theta_I(P_O)=\{(J_m(\widetilde{\mathsf P}))_{m\in\mathcal M}:
 \widetilde{\mathsf P}\in\mathfrak M_H,
 \ \widetilde{\mathsf P}_O=P_O\}                          \tag{1}
\]
from the observed-margin functional \(\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\).  We now prove their equality.

For any compatible law, the converse part of \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) produces \(\gamma\in\mathcal G_H(p_{BT},q)\), and its projection \(x_{bw}=\sum_t\gamma_{btw}\) belongs to \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\).  Since the \((B,T)\) margin is fixed,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 J_m
 &=\pi\,\mathsf E[T\mathbf 1\{B<m\}+W\mathbf 1\{B\ge m\}
                  \mid S_k^1=1]\\
 &=\pi\left[\sum_{b<m}\sum_ttp_{bt}
             +\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right]\\
 &=\pi\left[\sum_{b<m}\mu_b+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right].
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{2}
\]
Thus \(\Theta_I(P_O)\subseteq\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\).  Conversely, for every \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\), \(\text{lem:triple-projection-and-extension}\) supplies a compatible \(\gamma\), and the forward part of \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) supplies a law with the same observed pushforward and that triple margin.  Equation (2) then gives the corresponding point of \(\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\).  Hence
\[
 \Theta_I(P_O)=\mathcal V(p_{BT},q).                       \tag{3}
\]
This proves sharpness: every point of the displayed observed-law functional, not only every coordinate endpoint, is causally attainable.  Since \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) is a nonempty compact convex polytope and (2) is affine in \(x\), the set in (3) is compact and convex.

For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^{|\mathcal M|}\), expand a common-plan value vector using finite sums:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lambda^{\top}J(x)
 &=\pi\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\lambda_m\sum_{b<m}\mu_b
   +\pi\sum_{b,w}w x_{bw}
       \sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\lambda_m\mathbf 1\{b\ge m\}\\
 &=\pi\left[\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\lambda_m\sum_{b<m}\mu_b
   +\sum_{b,w}c_b(\lambda)w x_{bw}\right].
\end{aligned}                                             \tag{4}
\]
Taking the maximum over the compact polytope in (4) is exactly the formula \(h_{\mathcal V}(\lambda)\) in \(\text{def:support-function}\).

For pairwise differences, let \(v_b(x)=\sum_wwx_{bw}\).  If \(m<j\), cancellation outside rows \(m,\ldots,j-1\) in (2) gives
\[
 J_m(x)-J_j(x)
 =\pi\sum_{b=m}^{j-1}\{v_b(x)-\mu_b\}.                   \tag{5}
\]
Maximizing (5) gives the first displayed formula for \(D_{mj}\).  If \(m>j\), the same cancellation gives
\[
 J_m(x)-J_j(x)
 =\pi\sum_{b=j}^{m-1}\{\mu_b-v_b(x)\},                  \tag{6}
\]
and maximizing (6) gives the second formula; \(D_{mm}=0\) is immediate.  There is no sign theorem for an off-diagonal difference.  For example, take \(H=2\), \(p_1=1\), \(q_0=1\), \(p_{1,1}=1\), \(\pi=1\), and menu \(\{1,2\}\).  Capacity forces \(W=0\), so \(J_1=0\), \(J_2=1\), and \(D_{12}=-1\).

For a fixed deterministic threshold \(m\), its worst-case regret relative to the best member of the finite menu is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sup_{v\in\mathcal V}\{v_m-\min_{j\in\mathcal M}v_j\}
 &=\sup_{v\in\mathcal V}\max_{j\in\mathcal M}(v_m-v_j)\\
 &=\max_{j\in\mathcal M}\sup_{v\in\mathcal V}(v_m-v_j)
 =\max_{j\in\mathcal M}D_{mj}=R_m.
\end{aligned}                                             \tag{7}
\]
The interchange in (7) holds because the maximum is over a finite set: both sides equal the supremum over \(\mathcal V\times\mathcal M\).  The included comparator \(j=m\) gives \(R_m\ge0\).  Minimizing (7) over the finite menu proves that the complete deterministic minimax correspondence is \(\mathcal M^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m\), including all ties.

Finally, coordinatewise projection always gives
\[
 \mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subseteq
 \prod_{m\in\mathcal M}[\underline J_m,\overline J_m].    \tag{8}
\]
The inclusion can be strict because different coordinate extrema can require incompatible plans.  For a direct witness, take \(H=3\), \(p=(2/5,3/10,1/5,1/10)\), \(q=(3/10,3/10,1/5,1/5)\), \(\pi=1\), \(\mu=(0,7/20,7/40,0)\), and menu \(\{1,2,3\}\).  The feasible plan
\[
 x_{00}=1/5,\ x_{03}=1/5,\ x_{11}=1/10,\ x_{12}=1/5,
 \ x_{21}=1/5,\ x_{30}=1/10                              \tag{9}
\]
attains \(J_1=7/10\), while the feasible plan
\[
 x_{02}=1/5,\ x_{03}=1/5,\ x_{11}=3/10,
 \ x_{20}=1/5,\ x_{30}=1/10                              \tag{10}
\]
attains \(J_2=7/20\).  The endpoint inequalities follow directly from the capacity and column totals: the selected mass for threshold one cannot have expectation above \(7/10\), and the selected row \(b=2\) can be put at zero, so these are the respective coordinate extrema.  Were the product point \((J_1,J_2)=(7/10,7/20)\) generated by one plan, then \(v_2=0\) and \(v_1+v_2=7/10\), hence \(v_1=7/10\).  But row \(b=1\) has mass \(3/10\) and can use only \(w\le2\), so \(v_1\le(3/10)2=3/5<7/10\), a contradiction.  Thus (8) is sometimes strict.

Only the transport term in \(h_{\mathcal V}(\lambda)\) must be optimized, so abbreviate \(c_b=c_b(\lambda)\).  Feasibility of \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) implies the complementary Hall inequalities
\[
 \sum_{v=w}^{H}q_v\le\sum_{b=0}^{H-w}p_b,
 \qquad w=0,\ldots,H,                                    \tag{1}
\]
because columns \(v\ge w\) can receive mass only from rows \(b\le H-v\le H-w\).  When the algorithm reaches column \(w\), previously processed columns contain total mass \(\sum_{v>w}q_v\) and have consumed that amount only from currently eligible rows.  By (1), the residual capacity among those rows is at least
\[
 \sum_{b=0}^{H-w}p_b-\sum_{v>w}q_v\ge q_w.                \tag{2}
\]
Thus column \(w\) can always be filled.  After the final column, equality of total row and column mass forces all row capacities to be exhausted.  This proves feasibility, including zero margins and equality in (1).  It is also a self-contained proof of the staircase-feasibility fact attributed in the statement to Dahl's reversed-row formulation; no external theorem is used as a logical premise here.

We prove optimality by a finite exchange argument.  Consider the largest not-yet-fixed column \(w\), and let \(b\) be an eligible row with maximal coefficient among rows having residual capacity.  Start with an optimal residual plan.  If it does not allocate to \((b,w)\) as much as the greedy step does, then some positive mass in column \(w\) is assigned to another eligible row \(b'\), while an equal positive amount of the residual mass of row \(b\) is assigned to some column \(v<w\).  For
\[
 0<\delta\le\min\{x_{b'w},x_{bv}\},
\]
replace \(\delta\) units in cells \((b',w),(b,v)\) by \(\delta\) units in cells \((b,w),(b',v)\).  Both new cells are allowed: \(b\le H-w\), and \(b'\le H-w\le H-v\).  Margins are unchanged.  The objective change is
\[
 \delta\{c_bw+c_{b'}v-c_{b'}w-c_bv\}
 =\delta(c_b-c_{b'})(w-v)\ge0.                            \tag{3}
\]
Hence an optimal plan can be modified to agree with this greedy allocation.  Choose \(\delta\) to exhaust one of the two discrepant cells and repeat; finiteness of the table makes the process terminate.  Repeating for the next-highest coefficient row until column \(w\) is full, and then inducting on \(w=H,H-1,\ldots,0\), produces an optimal plan identical to the greedy plan.  The sign and ordering of the real numbers \(c_b\) never entered except through the comparison \(c_b\ge c_{b'}\), so signed and nonmonotone directions are covered.

Each positive allocation exhausts a residual row capacity or the current column, and the last allocation exhausts both.  There are \(H+1\) rows and \(H+1\) columns, so at most
\[
 (H+1)+(H+1)-1=2H+1                                      \tag{4}
\]
positive cells are created.  As \(w\) decreases, exactly one new row becomes eligible.  Insert that row once into a max-heap keyed by \(c_b\), remove a row once when its capacity is exhausted, and retain a partially used top row when a column is exhausted.  Thus there are \(O(H)\) heap operations, each costing \(O(\log H)\), and \(O(H)\) allocations.  The coefficients \(c_b=\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbf 1\{b\ge m\}\) are computed by one prefix scan in \(O(H)\) time because \(|\mathcal M|\le H\).  The total time is \(O(H\log H)\).  Substitution of the resulting optimal plan into \(\text{def:support-function}\) attains \(h_{\mathcal V}(\lambda)\).

All calculations are over exact rational numbers.  The Hall tail-prefix slacks for \(t=1,2,3\) are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 t&1&2&3\\ \hline
 \sum_{b\ge t}p_b&3/5&3/10&1/10\\
 \sum_{w\le3-t}q_w&4/5&3/5&3/10
 \end{array}                                               \tag{1}
\]
and are nonnegative, so the Ferrers polytope is nonempty.

For \(m=1\), \(L_1=2\), \(a_1=3/5\),
\[
 (A_0,A_1,A_2)=(1/10,3/10,3/5),\qquad
 (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(3/10,3/5,4/5).
\]
Therefore
\[
 (Z_{1s}^{-})_{s=0}^2=(3/10,3/5,3/5),\qquad
 (Z_{1s}^{+})_{s=0}^2=(1/10,2/5,3/5).                     \tag{2}
\]
The endpoint theorem and \(\mu_0=0\) give
\[
 J_1\in\left[2(3/5)-(3/10+3/5),
               2(3/5)-(1/10+2/5)\right]=[3/10,7/10].     \tag{3}
\]
For \(m=2\), \(L_2=1\), \(a_2=3/10\),
\[
 (A_0,A_1)=(1/10,3/10),\qquad (Q_0,Q_1)=(3/10,3/5),
\]
so \(Z_{20}^{-}=3/10\), \(Z_{20}^{+}=1/10\).  Since \(\sum_{b<2}\mu_b=7/20\),
\[
 J_2\in[7/20,7/20+1/5]=[7/20,11/20].                     \tag{4}
\]
For \(m=3\), capacity forces the selected row \(b=3\) into column zero, and
\[
 J_3=\mu_0+\mu_1+\mu_2=7/20+7/40=21/40.                  \tag{5}
\]

For completeness, the exact shell extrema delivered by the eligibility-greedy theorem are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
 E&\min_{x\in\Gamma_3}\sum_{b\in E,w}wx_{bw}
  &\max_{x\in\Gamma_3}\sum_{b\in E,w}wx_{bw}\\ \hline
 \{1\}&1/10&1/2\\
 \{2\}&0&1/5\\
 \{1,2\}&3/10&7/10.
 \end{array}                                               \tag{6}
\]
These values also have short direct certificates.  Row \(3\) forces mass \(1/10\) into column zero, so row \(1\) can put at most \(1/5\) of its mass at zero, proving its expectation is at least \(1/10\); the plan with row \(1\) masses \(1/5\) at zero and \(1/10\) at one attains it.  For the maximum, column two has mass \(1/5\), so row \(1\) puts at most \(1/5\) there and its remaining \(1/10\) at at most one, giving \(1/2\), which is attainable.  Row \(2\) has mass \(1/5\) and ceiling one, giving the second row of (6), with both zero and one assignments feasible.  The last row of (6) is equivalently (3) before the zero continued-treatment term.  Thus (6) is certified by inequalities and feasible allocations, not only by an optimization assertion.

Applying the pairwise identities to (6) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_{12}&=1/2-7/20=3/20,&
 D_{13}&=7/10-(7/20+7/40)=7/40,\\
 D_{21}&=7/20-1/10=1/4,&
 D_{23}&=1/5-7/40=1/40,\\
 D_{31}&=7/20+7/40-3/10=9/40,&
 D_{32}&=7/40-0=7/40,
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{7}
\]
with zero diagonal.  Hence
\[
 (R_1,R_2,R_3)=(7/40,1/4,9/40),
 \qquad \mathcal M^\star=\{1\}.                          \tag{8}
\]

Using the separate sharp intervals (3)--(5), the off-diagonal box differences give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R_1^{\Box}&=\max\{0,7/10-7/20,7/10-21/40\}=7/20,\\
 R_2^{\Box}&=\max\{11/20-3/10,0,11/20-21/40\}=1/4,\\
 R_3^{\Box}&=\max\{21/40-3/10,21/40-7/20,0\}=9/40.
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{9}
\]
The smallest number in (9) is uniquely \(9/40\), so \(\mathcal M^{\Box}=\{3\}\).  Equations (3)--(9) prove every assertion.

At \(\mathsf E_3\), the three nontrivial Hall slacks, in the order \(t=1,2,3\), are
\[
 (1/5,3/10,1/5),                                           \tag{1}
\]
as computed in the rational proposition.  They are strictly positive.  Each slack is a linear, hence continuous, function of \((p,q)\).

We next verify continuity of every decision quantity used in the claim without assuming differentiability or a fixed active transport basis.  For a fixed coefficient vector \(c=(c_b)_{b=0}^3\), the eligibility-greedy algorithm computes
\[
 \phi_c(p,q)=\max_{x\in\Gamma_3(p,q)}\sum_{b,w}c_bw x_{bw}. \tag{2}
\]
Fix a deterministic tie-breaking order for equal \(c_b\).  The algorithm has only finitely many possible row- or column-exhaustion patterns.  On each pattern its allocations are obtained from the margins by finitely many additions, subtractions, and minima, and are therefore continuous and piecewise affine.  When a pattern changes, the allocation causing the change is zero at the common boundary, so the adjacent objective formulas agree.  Thus \(\phi_c\) is continuous on the feasible margin domain near \(\mathsf E_3\).  Minima are covered by
\[
 \min_{x\in\Gamma_3(p,q)}\sum_{b,w}c_bw x_{bw}=-\phi_{-c}(p,q). \tag{3}
\]
The endpoint formulas use only finite sums, minima, and maxima, and hence are continuous as well.  The pairwise differences are finite sums of \(\mu_b\), multiplied by \(\pi\), plus an extremum of the form (2) or (3).  Therefore every \(D_{mj}\), every \(D_{mj}^{\Box}\), every finite maximum \(R_m\) or \(R_m^{\Box}\), and every endpoint is continuous in \((\pi,p,\mu,q)\) on \(\Theta_3\) near \(\mathsf E_3\).

At the center point, the strict common-law-versus-box gap is
\[
 D_{12}^{\Box}-D_{12}=7/20-3/20=1/5.                      \tag{4}
\]
The shared-law regret vector and its gaps above the first coordinate are
\[
 (R_1,R_2,R_3)=(7/40,1/4,9/40),\qquad
 R_2-R_1=3/40,\quad R_3-R_1=1/20.                          \tag{5}
\]
The box regret vector and its gaps above the third coordinate are
\[
 (R_1^{\Box},R_2^{\Box},R_3^{\Box})=(7/20,1/4,9/40),
 \qquad R_1^{\Box}-R_3^{\Box}=1/8,\quad
 R_2^{\Box}-R_3^{\Box}=1/40.                              \tag{6}
\]
All quantities in (1), (4), (5), and (6) are strictly positive.  By the finite intersection of their continuity neighborhoods, there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that every point of \(\Theta_3\) within sup-norm distance \(\varepsilon\) retains their signs.  Shrinking \(\varepsilon\) if necessary also retains \(\pi>0\) and the positive margin coordinates of the center.  Equations (1), (5), and (6) then prove, respectively, strict nontrivial Hall inequalities, \(\mathcal M^\star=\{1\}\), and \(\mathcal M^{\Box}=\{3\}\), while (4) proves \(D_{12}<D_{12}^{\Box}\).

For any feasible set \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^3\), equality with the product of its coordinate intervals would imply
\[
 \sup_{v\in V}(v_1-v_2)=\sup_{v\in V}v_1-\inf_{v\in V}v_2. \tag{7}
\]
For \(V=\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\), the two sides of (7) are \(D_{12}\) and \(D_{12}^{\Box}\).  Their strict inequality therefore proves
\[
 \mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subsetneq
 \prod_{m\in\mathcal M}[\underline J_m,\overline J_m].    \tag{8}
\]
Finally, the formulas for the value set and pairwise differences depend on the full array \(p_{bt}\) only through its row masses \(p_b\) and first-moment masses \(\mu_b=\sum_ttp_{bt}\).  Hence the same \(\varepsilon\) works simultaneously for every \(p_{bt}\) having the stipulated row sums and moments.  The intersection of the sup-norm ball with \(\Theta_3\) is relatively open and contains \(\mathsf E_3\), proving the claimed nondegenerate family.

Let
\[
 \mathcal E_{n,\alpha}=\{(r_{bt},q_w)\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}. \tag{1}
\]
By hypothesis, \(\mathsf P(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha})\ge1-\alpha\).  Work on this event and fix any conditional transport \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\).  Define the unconditional perspective quantities
\[
 r_{bt}=\pi p_{bt},\qquad s_w=\pi q_w,\qquad
 \widetilde x_{bw}=\pi x_{bw}.                             \tag{2}
\]
Because \(\pi=\sum_{b,t}r_{bt}\in(0,1]\), membership in the rectangle in (1) gives the cellwise constraints on \(r\), and
\[
 \underline q_w\sum_{b,t}r_{bt}\le s_w
 \le\overline q_w\sum_{b,t}r_{bt}.                        \tag{3}
\]
The transport margins and support give
\[
 \sum_w\widetilde x_{bw}=\pi p_b=\sum_tr_{bt},\qquad
 \sum_b\widetilde x_{bw}=\pi q_w=s_w,\qquad
 \widetilde x_{bw}=0\ \text{if }b+w>H.                   \tag{4}
\]
Equations (2)--(4), together with nonnegativity, show
\[
 (\mathbf r,\mathbf s,\widetilde{\mathbf x})
 \in\widehat{\mathcal P}_{n,\alpha}.                     \tag{5}
\]
Its image under \(\text{def:value-confidence-set}\) has coordinate
\[
 \sum_{b<m,t}tr_{bt}+\sum_{b\ge m,w}w\widetilde x_{bw}
 =\pi\left[\sum_{b<m}\mu_b+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right]. \tag{6}
\]
By the joint sharp-identification theorem, as \(x\) ranges over \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\), (6) ranges over the entire causal identified set \(\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\).  Since (5) holds for every such \(x\),
\[
 \mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal V}_{n,\alpha}
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}.                   \tag{7}
\]

For optimizer coverage, first note that \(\pi>0\) makes scaling bijective:
\[
 \mathsf X_H(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)
 =\{\pi x:x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\}.                           \tag{8}
\]
Substituting (8) into \(\mathsf J_m\) gives
\[
 \mathsf D_{mj}(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)=D_{mj},\qquad
 \mathsf R_m(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)=R_m                    \tag{9}
\]
at the true perspective margins.  Those margins belong to the projection of the confidence polytope by (5).  Therefore, simultaneously for every \(m\),
\[
 \underline R_m^{n,\alpha}\le R_m\le\overline R_m^{n,\alpha}. \tag{10}
\]
If \(m\in\mathcal M^\star\), then \(R_m=\min_jR_j\).  Using (10) for every \(j\),
\[
 \underline R_m^{n,\alpha}\le R_m=\min_jR_j
 \le\min_j\overline R_j^{n,\alpha},                      \tag{11}
\]
so \(m\in\widehat{\mathcal M}_{n,\alpha}\).  This proves
\[
 \mathcal M^\star\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal M}_{n,\alpha}
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}.                   \tag{12}
\]
No step made a Hall inequality or a regret comparison strict, and (11) retains every tied minimizer.

On the event (1) the confidence polytope is nonempty by (5).  It is closed and bounded: its nonnegative total mass is at most one, and the row and column equations bound \(s\) and \(x\) by the same total.  Thus it and its projections are compact polytopes.  The value image is linear.  Each \(\mathsf D_{mj}\) is the optimum of a finite transport program over the explicitly displayed polytope \(\mathsf X_H(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)\), and the remaining minima and maxima range over a finite menu and the compact projected confidence polytope.  Hence all reported sets and envelopes are computable finite-dimensional optimization objects.  Taking probabilities in (7) and (12) completes both \(1-\alpha\) coverage claims.

theorem.statement: The finite-dimensional inversion has the following exact scope.  If the first-stage regions satisfy \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\mathsf P\in\mathfrak M_H}\mathsf P\{((r_{bt}),(q_w))\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}\ge1-\alpha\), then \(\text{thm:confidence-polytope}\) gives the same uniform asymptotic outer coverage for \(\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\) and \(\mathcal M^\star\), including simultaneous Hall equalities and arbitrary policy ties.  However, coarsening at random, pointwise censoring positivity, and the phrase ``multiply robust nuisance estimation'' alone cannot yield nonvacuous uniformly shrinking inference.  For every \(H\ge2\) and \(0<\alpha<1/2\), any uniformly honest sequence of observed-data confidence regions for the whole value set has a sequence of laws in \(\mathfrak M_H\) along which its sup-norm diameter is at least \(H\) with limiting probability at least \(1-2\alpha\).  Already for \(H=3\) and \(\mathcal M=\{1,2,3\}\), any uniformly honest outer confidence set for \(\mathcal M^\star\) has a sequence along which it contains both thresholds \(1\) and \(3\) with limiting probability at least \(1-2\alpha\).  Thus a nonvacuous cross-fitted implementation of \(\mathfrak I\) requires quantitative conditions that exclude the displayed vanishing-information sequences and control nuisance remainders; standard sufficient conditions would include uniform effective assignment, survival, and censoring overlap together with uniform cross-fitted rate conditions, none of which is supplied by the frozen assumptions.
theorem.proof_tex:
The positive conditional statement follows immediately from event inclusion.  For every \(\mathsf P\in\mathfrak M_H\), the proof of \(\text{thm:confidence-polytope}\) shows
\[
 \{(r,q)\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}
 \subseteq
 \{\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal V}_{n,\alpha},\ 
   \mathcal M^\star\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal M}_{n,\alpha}\}. \tag{1}
\]
Taking probabilities, then the infimum over \(\mathfrak M_H\), and then the lower limit proves the asserted uniform coverage.  The proof of (1) is set-theoretic, so neither a unique active Hall face nor a unique policy optimizer is required.

We now prove that the frozen assumptions do not provide a nonvacuous uniform first stage.  Fix \(H\ge2\), let \(\epsilon_n=n^{-2}\), and consider two laws with no death, landmark survival one, \(B=0\), and switched residual \(W=0\).  Under the first law the sustained intensive residual is \(T=0\) almost surely; under the second it is \(T=H\) almost surely.  Give both arms positive randomization probability, for example one half.  Let every subject be observed through \(k\); independently of the response tree, continue observation through \(K\) with probability \(\epsilon_n\), and otherwise censor at \(k\).  Conditional on continuation, retain observation through \(K\).  Every continuation probability appearing in the frozen censoring-positivity assumption is strictly positive for each \(n\), and independence makes censoring exchangeability hold.  The remaining causal restrictions hold because \(B+W=0\le H\), the switched \(W\) margin equals the standard residual margin concentrated at zero, and legal response trees are obtained by the construction in \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\).

For every threshold \(m\in\mathcal M\subseteq\{1,\ldots,H\}\), \(B<m\).  Hence the two sharp value sets are the distinct singletons
\[
 V_0=\{(0)_{m\in\mathcal M}\},\qquad
 V_1=\{(H)_{m\in\mathcal M}\}.                           \tag{2}
\]
Couple one observation under the two laws by using the same assignment, censoring indicator, and all pre-\(k\) data.  The coupled observations can differ only if an intensive-arm subject is followed through \(K\), an event of probability at most \(\epsilon_n\).  For \(n\) independent observations, the union bound therefore gives
\[
 \left\|P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}-P_{1,n}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le n\epsilon_n=n^{-1}\longrightarrow0.                 \tag{3}
\]
Here (3) follows directly from the displayed coupling: total variation is at most the probability that the coupled samples differ.

Let \((\mathcal C_n)\) be any observed-data random sets with uniform asymptotic whole-set coverage at level \(1-\alpha\).  Uniformity applies to both triangular sequences, so
\[
 P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}(V_0\subseteq\mathcal C_n)\ge1-\alpha-o(1),
 \qquad
 P_{1,n}^{\otimes n}(V_1\subseteq\mathcal C_n)\ge1-\alpha-o(1). \tag{4}
\]
By (3), the second event in (4) has probability at least \(1-\alpha-o(1)\) under \(P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}\) as well.  The union bound under that common law yields
\[
 P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}\{V_0\cup V_1\subseteq\mathcal C_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-o(1).                                       \tag{5}
\]
On the event in (5), \(\operatorname{diam}_{\infty}(\mathcal C_n)\ge H\) by (2).  This proves the value-set impossibility certificate.

For the optimizer certificate, specialize to \(H=3\), \(\mathcal M=\{1,2,3\}\), and use the common \((p,q)\) margins of \(\mathsf E_3\).  In the first law take \(T=0\) conditional on every \(B\).  The shell extrema in the eligibility-greedy proof give
\[
 (R_1,R_2,R_3)=(7/10,1/5,0),\qquad \mathcal M^\star=\{3\}. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, with every \(\mu_b=0\), threshold three has no positive worst-case difference, while the displayed maxima for shells \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{2\}\) give the first two entries.  In the second law use the conditional \(T\) distribution realizing \(\mathsf E_3\): on row \(1\), put conditional probabilities \(5/6\) and \(1/6\) at \(T=1,2\); on row \(2\), put probabilities \(1/8\) and \(7/8\) at \(T=0,1\); and put \(T=0\) on rows \(0,3\).  This gives \((\mu_0,\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3)=(0,7/20,7/40,0)\), and \(\text{prop:rational-recommendation-reversal}\) gives \(\mathcal M^\star=\{1\}\).

Apply the same censoring scheme with continuation probability \(\epsilon_n\).  Before \(k\) the two laws have the same \(B\) distribution, and their standard histories and switched margins are identical; their observed data can differ only for a continued intensive-arm observation.  Thus the total-variation bound (3) holds again.  If \((\mathcal K_n)\) is any uniformly honest optimizer outer confidence set, coverage under the two laws and the same transfer-plus-union-bound argument give
\[
 P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}\{\{1,3\}\subseteq\mathcal K_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-o(1).                                       \tag{7}
\]
This is an explicit generic-class obstruction, and it occurs with strict Hall slack and unique optimizers.  Therefore Hall equalities and policy ties are not the obstacle; the missing premise is quantitative uniform information in the censored histories.  Any nonvacuous positive theorem must at least exclude the displayed vanishing-censoring sequence and control its nuisance remainders.  Uniform lower bounds on the relevant effective assignment, survival, and censoring probabilities, together with explicit cross-fitted nuisance convergence and second-order remainder controls, are standard sufficient hypotheses of that kind.  Since the frozen core states no quantitative overlap or rate condition, the proposed cross-fitted guarantee cannot honestly be derived from it.

proposed.statement: Assume \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\ne\varnothing\). For every \(m\in\mathcal M\), the attainable selected-column subdistributions \(z_w\) are exactly those satisfying \(z_w=0\) for \(w>L_m\), \(0\le z_w\le q_w\), \(\sum_{w=0}^{L_m}z_w=a_m\), and \(\sum_{w=0}^{s}z_w\ge A_s\) for \(0\le s\le L_m\). Their pointwise maximal and minimal cumulative arrays are respectively \(Z_{ms}^{-}\) and \(Z_{ms}^{+}\) from \(\text{def:threshold-cumulative-envelopes}\). In particular, \(Z_{m,L_m}^{-}=Z_{m,L_m}^{+}=a_m\) and \(Z_{ms}^{+}=\max\{A_s,Z_{m,s+1}^{+}-q_{s+1}\}\) for \(s<L_m\). Consequently, \(\inf_{x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)}\sum_{b\ge m,w}w x_{bw}=L_ma_m-\sum_{s=0}^{L_m-1}Z_{ms}^{-}\) and \(\sup_{x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)}\sum_{b\ge m,w}w x_{bw}=L_ma_m-\sum_{s=0}^{L_m-1}Z_{ms}^{+}\), with both endpoints attained. The sharp endpoints for \(J_m\) add \(\pi\sum_{b<m}\mu_b\) and multiply the displayed selected contribution by \(\pi\).
proposed.justification: Dahl2008, Theorem 4, supplies the attributed feasibility support; the new closed forms expose the backward capacity deficit that unrestricted sum bounds omit and permit exact threshold comparisons without repeated linear programs.
proposed.gap: ZhangRichardson2025 resolves discrete sharpness for unrestricted fixed-marginal sums; the support deletion \(b+w>H\) changes both feasibility and the upper endpoint through the backward deficit.
proposed.consumer: JanvinRyalenSarvetStensrud2025's fixed-threshold switching loss becomes sharply bounded in an externally prespecified capacity-sensitivity analysis.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The transport derivation alone proves attained extrema over \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\), but the target calls the resulting \(J_m\) endpoints causally sharp. Adding the triple-extension and observed-law-preserving lift as explicit dependencies declares the required causal-attainment spine without changing the claim.
